report.summary: Industry standard (AWS IAM, Cedar, common OPA patterns) mandates explicit deny takes precedence over any allow, regardless of evaluation order. 'Exceptions before denies' (allow-overrides) is rarely defensible; it risks project-scoped allows shadowing baseline denies, leading to unintended access and privilege escalation. Recommend deny-overrides default.
risks: Allow-overrides model can cause privilege escalation if a project-scoped allow list inadvertently permits access blocked by a baseline deny.
Maintaining security posture becomes harder when local exceptions can override global safeguards.
Order-dependent evaluation ('first match') can lead to inconsistent policy interpretations and bypasses.
todos: Adopt explicit deny precedence: deny always wins over allow, regardless of declaration order.
Ensure the evaluation engine returns 'deny' if any applicable policy yields an explicit deny, else 'allow' if any allows and no denies, else 'deny'.
Audit existing allow lists to verify they cannot circumvent baseline denies under the new precedence.
Document the precedence rule clearly in project guidelines and architecture decision records.

references: Cedar (Amazon Verified Permissions) docs: Forbid always takes precedence over Permit.
OPA policy language: deny-overrides pattern using 'default deny = false' and explicit deny rules.
handoff.suggestion: Implement an explicit deny resolver that short-circuits evaluation once a deny is found, similar to AWS IAM's model. This aligns with Daedalus' fail-closed egress fence.

name: q07-policy-evaluation-order
question: Policy-engine evaluation order: is 'exceptions evaluated before denies' ever a defensible default, and what do AWS IAM, Cedar and OPA/Rego mandate about explicit-deny precedence? What goes wrong when a project-scoped allow list can shadow a baseline deny?
